title: AI in education is becoming a governance and human-capability question, not merely a technology-adoption question
source_unit: UNESCO Institute for Information Technologies in Education, 2026 GSE Annual Report: Smart Education Around the World
geography: Seven world regions and diverse national education systems integrating AI and digital technologies across differing social, economic, and institutional contexts

core_integration.value: pedagogy, governance, and technology are integrated to make learning systems more responsive to learners, teachers, and societies

purpose_priority.value: educational purpose is placed at the centre so technology serves learning, strengthens human capabilities, and supports sustainable development

scope_boundary.value: Smart Education goes beyond adopting digital technologies or AI tools alone

observations.method: UNESCO IITE synthesis of seven regional reports and partner perspectives on integrating AI and digital technologies in education.
observations.uncertainty: The framework is normative and comparative; it does not estimate learning effects, define a single implementation score, or establish that integrated systems improve outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Learners, teachers, schools, education ministries, technology providers, families, and societies with different infrastructure and governance conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Technology can support learning and teacher work, but expanding tools without pedagogy, support, accessibility, privacy, and accountability may deepen inequity or add workload.

observations.period: 2026; regional variation in AI and digital education integration

denominator.unit: world regions examined through partner regional reports

regional_pathways.value: there is no single pathway to Smart Education

national_platforms.value: some systems use national digital platforms serving millions of learners

fragile_contexts.value: in other contexts Smart Education includes maintaining learning in fragile environments

teacher_support.value: some systems focus on supporting teachers with new tools

observations.method: Cross-regional synthesis of partner perspectives and regional reports rather than a uniform country scorecard.
observations.uncertainty: Examples illustrate variation but do not establish prevalence, comparative effectiveness, or the number of countries using each pathway.
observations.subgroup: Education systems with different levels of connectivity, conflict exposure, public capacity, language, financing, and teacher workforce support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different pathways may reflect adaptation to context rather than unequal ambition; large platforms can scale access while also creating dependency, privacy, or governance risks.

observations.period: 2026; AI education opportunity and responsibility frame

denominator.unit: UNESCO IITE assessment of AI's role in education systems

opportunity.value: AI can expand learning opportunities and support more responsive education systems

responsibility.value: AI adoption creates new responsibilities for education systems to preserve human values

human_capabilities.value: technology should strengthen human capabilities rather than displace educational purpose

observations.method: UNESCO IITE policy synthesis connecting AI opportunity, human values, learning purpose, and institutional responsibility.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not provide a causal model for AI and learning or a common definition of human-value preservation across systems.
observations.subgroup: Students, teachers, administrators, education policymakers, parents, technology designers, and communities affected by AI-mediated learning.
observations.counterinterpretation: Human-centred AI can still reproduce bias or surveillance through data, procurement, language, or assessment systems unless governance is operational and contestable.

denominator.unit: regional perspectives synthesized in the annual report

shared_aspiration.value: education systems seek to use digital technology to expand opportunity while preserving human values

shared_lesson.value: technology integration must be read through pedagogy, governance, teacher capacity, social context, and sustainability

institutional_question.value: the central question is how AI can be harnessed responsibly rather than whether AI will influence education

observations.method: UNESCO IITE cross-regional comparison of partner findings and policy experiences.
observations.uncertainty: Shared lessons are a synthesis across selected regional materials and do not represent all education systems or prove policy transferability.
observations.subgroup: National and local education authorities, teachers, learners, families, technology partners, and vulnerable or disconnected communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Common principles may mask real conflicts over curriculum, data ownership, language, teacher autonomy, commercial influence, and the distribution of benefits.

related_sources.claim: UNESCO GEM 2026 provides complementary global education access and equity trends.
UNESCO IITE publication catalog for digital education and information-technology research.

boundary: This record adds an education-technology governance route linking AI, pedagogy, teacher capacity, infrastructure, fragile contexts, equity, human values, sustainability, and institutional responsibility. It is a cross-regional policy synthesis, not student-level learning data, a technology-adoption census, a causal effect estimate, a school implementation audit, or proof that Smart Education improves outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: UNESCO IITE official publication page was reviewed for the Smart Education definition, seven-region scope, examples of national platforms and fragile-context learning, AI opportunity and responsibility, and shared lessons.
